nameStory: The name 'charlock' comes from the Old English 'cerlice,' referring to this wild mustard that commonly invaded grain fields. Farmers knew it well as a persistent weed that would spring up among their crops, earning it the alternative name 'field mustard' for its habit of appearing wherever soil was disturbed.
description: Charlock is a scrappy annual wildflower that looks like a wild version of the mustard you might grow in your garden. This upright plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall with bright yellow, four-petaled flowers clustered at the top of branching stems. Its leaves are roughly toothed and somewhat hairy, giving the whole plant a slightly rough, weedy appearance that's common among plants that thrive in disturbed soils.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four petals arranged in a cross pattern, typical of the mustard family. Each flower is about half an inch across and has a faint, sweet fragrance when you get close.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are deeply lobed and feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch, while upper leaves are smaller and less divided. All leaves have irregular, coarse teeth along their edges.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops long, narrow seed pods (called siliques) that are bumpy and constricted between the seeds, looking almost beaded. These pods feel firm and make a slight rattling sound when mature and dry.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright, branching plant with multiple flower clusters at the stem tips. The whole plant has a somewhat coarse, weedy appearance and often grows in patches.

habitat: Look for charlock in disturbed soils like roadsides, abandoned fields, construction sites, and agricultural edges throughout New England. It thrives in sunny locations with rich, loose soil and is often found mixed with other weedy plants like dandelions and plantains. This plant particularly loves areas where the ground has been recently turned or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early and begin developing their characteristic lobed basal leaves. Plants that overwintered as seedlings start their rapid growth spurt.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flower clusters most visible from June through August. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and developing seed pods may be present.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and dry out, becoming brown and papery. Plants begin to die back, but dried stems with empty pods may persist.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants are dead, but some seeds may germinate late in the season to overwinter as small rosettes in milder areas.

funFact: Charlock seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to 60 years, which explains why this plant can suddenly appear in huge numbers when old farmland is disturbed, sprouting from seeds that may have been buried since before you were born!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other yellow-flowered mustards, but charlock's bumpy, beaded seed pods are distinctive. Remember: 'charlock's pods look like little necklaces' - those constrictions between seeds make them stand out from the smooth pods of many other mustards.
contextualKnowledge: There's some taxonomic confusion with this plant - you might see it listed under different scientific names (Brassica arvensis or Sinapis arvensis) in older field guides. All refer to the same weedy mustard that farmers have been dealing with for centuries.
compareHints: Charlock differs from its relative black mustard by having much more obvious bumps and constrictions in its seed pods, while black mustard pods are smooth and pressed close to the stem. Charlock's flowers are also typically larger and brighter yellow, and its leaves feel rougher and hairier to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black mustard differs from its close relative charlock mainly in how the seed pods attach to the stem - black mustard pods press tightly against the stem while charlock pods spread outward at angles.
